lines.text: Lesson 1 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/01_requirements_to_architecture.py
Why this matters
Architecture starts before a service name. A good design turns business outcomes and non-functional requirements
into explicit data contracts, latency targets, security boundaries, recovery goals and cost constraints. If you jump
straight from 'we need a dashboard' to a list of products, the diagram may look professional while answering the
wrong problem.
Picture it in your head
Picture a bridge engineer. Before choosing steel thickness, they need span, traffic, wind, maintenance access and
acceptable failure behavior. Data architecture is the same translation problem: requirements become forces on the
design.
New words before we use them

rows: What the system must do for users or downstream systems.
How well or under what constraints the system must operate, such as latency, reliability, security or cost.
A formal or internal service target used to reason about acceptable performance/reliability.
A boundary the design must respect, such as budget, region, team skill or compliance.
A deliberate gain in one property that usually costs something elsewhere.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Start with six questions: who consumes the data, what decision/action depends on it, how fresh it must be, how
wrong it may be before harm occurs, what data is sensitive, and what failure/recovery window is acceptable. Then
add volume and growth. Only after these are explicit should you compare architecture options. Separate facts from
guesses: '20 million events/day today' is evidence; 'will probably double' is an assumption that should be tested with a
scenario rather than treated as truth.
A second architecture-review lens
A reviewer should be able to point to every box and ask which requirement forced it to exist. If the answer is only 'best
practice', the design is not yet grounded. Separate hard constraints from preferences: residency law or RPO zero
may be hard; a preferred cloud service may be negotiable. Also record revisit triggers, such as volume crossing 5x,
latency tightening below one minute, or the team gaining platform support. Architecture is a current decision under
stated conditions, not a permanent truth.

Follow with me once
A retailer wants hourly store sales by 07:00 local time, can tolerate 30 minutes of delay during recovery, must keep
cardholder data out of analytics, and has a two-person data team. Translate this into: batch ingestion every 15
minutes or hourly, curated sales grain, PII tokenization before analytics, a published freshness SLO, replayable raw
evidence, simple managed components, and an alert if reconciliation or freshness fails. Notice that the requirements
already rule out some unnecessarily complex designs.
What you should see / why it worked
An architecture decision sheet linking each important requirement to a design response and a measurable proof.
Another engineer should be able to disagree with your choice without first guessing your assumptions. The important
part is the trace from requirement to decision to evidence; the same product name can be correct in one requirement
set and wrong in another.
Break it: a realistic failure
A team selects Kafka, Spark, Kubernetes and a lakehouse because these technologies appear in job descriptions.
The workload is one 2 GB nightly file with next-morning reporting. The result creates 24x7 operating cost and a steep
on-call burden without a requirement that needs streaming or cluster orchestration.
Reason through a realistic incident
Preserve the evidence first. State the violated requirement, then identify the smallest failing boundary. Separate
business-data state from compute/configuration/identity state. Bound the blast radius, choose a reversible repair,
validate the original requirement, and finally test a changed case. Architecture recovery should reduce uncertainty,
not hide it behind more components.
Now you do a changed version alone
Use the supplied clinic-reporting scenario. Write functional requirements, at least six non-functional requirements,
known constraints, assumptions, and three questions you still need from stakeholders. Sketch a first architecture only
after those are written.
Fresh changed retry
Change the requirement from 'next morning' to 'fraud alert within 10 seconds' and explain exactly which architecture
boundaries must change and which can remain batch.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when your decision cites a requirement/constraint and an independent control or measurement.
• If a fact is unknown, label it as an assumption and state what you would measure before committing.
• Reject a design that solves the happy path but has no replay/recovery, ownership, security boundary or cost story.
• After repair/review, change latency, volume, budget or compliance and prove you can adapt instead of reciting the
same diagram.
Ready-made revision
From requirements to architecture is a decision problem. Remember the requirement, the competing options, the
trade-off, the failure boundary and the evidence that would validate the choice.
Teach it back
Explain why architecture is primarily a requirements-to-trade-offs exercise rather than a cloud-service memorization
exercise.
Evidence / mastery
Save your first architecture/scorecard, reviewer challenge, corrected decision, changed-case retry, and a short ADR
explaining why you chose one option over another. Do not erase the first design when you improve it.
Lesson 2 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/02_batch_streaming_decision.py
Why this matters
Streaming is valuable when action loses value quickly, but it adds continuous state, ordering, replay, capacity and
operational concerns. Batch is not 'old technology'; it is often the safest choice when latency requirements permit it.
The architecture skill is choosing the simplest model that meets the decision deadline.
Picture it in your head
Mail delivery versus a live phone call. Both move information. A monthly statement does not need a live call;
emergency dispatch does. The delivery mode should match the consequence of waiting.
New words before we use them

rows: How long the business can wait before data must influence an action.
When the business event actually happened.
When the system handled the event.
Reprocessing retained events after failure or logic correction.
An architecture intentionally combining streaming and batch paths.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Use a decision tree instead of fashion. Ask: what is the maximum useful delay? Is the source naturally event-driven?
Must individual events trigger actions, or are periodic aggregates enough? Can downstream consumers handle
continuous updates? What replay and state semantics are required? A 5-minute dashboard might still be
micro-batch. A stream can also feed a durable batch/lakehouse path for reconciliation and reprocessing.
A second architecture-review lens
The hardest part is often not choosing batch or stream, but defining the consistency boundary between them. A
streaming alert can be provisional while an hourly reconciliation becomes the accounting truth. That is acceptable
when consumers know the contract. Conversely, two paths that silently compute the same metric differently create
permanent reconciliation debt. If you design a hybrid path, name which system owns final truth, how late corrections
flow, and how replay avoids double effects.

Follow with me once
Compare three workloads. Payroll: monthly, correctness dominates latency - batch. Card fraud: suspicious
transaction must be acted on in seconds - streaming event path plus durable replay. Executive daily revenue: source
events may arrive continuously, but a governed hourly/daily aggregate can remain batch or micro-batch. The same
company can rationally use all three.
What you should see / why it worked
A latency/value table and a justified choice that names state, replay, ordering and operational implications - not
merely 'streaming is faster'. The important part is the trace from requirement to decision to evidence; the same
product name can be correct in one requirement set and wrong in another.
Break it: a realistic failure
A product team asks for 'real time' because the phrase sounds modern. No one can identify a user action that
changes within an hour. The stream becomes a permanent on-call system while reports are opened once each
morning.
Reason through a realistic incident
Preserve the evidence first. State the violated requirement, then identify the smallest failing boundary. Separate
business-data state from compute/configuration/identity state. Bound the blast radius, choose a reversible repair,
validate the original requirement, and finally test a changed case. Architecture recovery should reduce uncertainty,
not hide it behind more components.
Now you do a changed version alone
Classify six supplied workloads as batch, micro-batch, streaming or hybrid. For each, give the decision deadline,
replay expectation and one failure mode.
Fresh changed retry
Take one batch choice and tighten its useful latency by 100x. Re-evaluate source, storage, compute and monitoring
without automatically assuming every component must become streaming.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when your decision cites a requirement/constraint and an independent control or measurement.
• If a fact is unknown, label it as an assumption and state what you would measure before committing.
• Reject a design that solves the happy path but has no replay/recovery, ownership, security boundary or cost story.
• After repair/review, change latency, volume, budget or compliance and prove you can adapt instead of reciting the
same diagram.

trade-off, the failure boundary and the evidence that would validate the choice.
Teach it back

Lesson 3 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/03_warehouse_lakehouse_decision.py
Why this matters
Warehouse and lakehouse are not team identities; they are serving/storage patterns with different strengths. A
warehouse often gives strong governed SQL analytics and operational simplicity. A lakehouse brings
open-file/object-storage economics with table semantics and multi-engine flexibility. Many production platforms use
both patterns or products that blur the boundary.
Picture it in your head
Think of a highly organized library versus a warehouse-sized archive with a catalog and table system layered over it.
The right question is what kinds of readers, formats, transformations and governance you need - not which label
sounds newer.
New words before we use them

rows: Analytical database pattern optimized for governed SQL/BI workloads.
Architecture combining lake/object-storage openness with table-management/warehouse-like capabilities.
Metadata/protocol layer that gives files table semantics such as versions and transactions.
Data representation designed for a consumer/query pattern.
Keeping one type of workload from unpredictably harming another.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Compare on workload and operating model: BI concurrency, semi/unstructured data, open engine access, ML/Spark
needs, governance, cost model, performance predictability and team skills. Do not treat 'cheap storage' as 'cheap
system': query engines, compaction, cataloging and operational labor matter. Likewise, do not assume a warehouse
cannot ingest files or a lakehouse cannot serve SQL; modern products overlap.
A second architecture-review lens
Think in data products and workload boundaries rather than brand categories. Raw evidence may live cheaply in
object storage while governed serving data uses an engine optimized for concurrent SQL. The same
Delta/Iceberg-style table may be queried by multiple engines, yet each query engine still has capacity, security and
cost behavior. Your decision should include who owns table maintenance, catalog policy, semantic definitions and
performance expectations; storage format alone does not solve those responsibilities.

validate the original requirement, and finally test a changed case. Architecture recovery should reduce uncertainty,
not hide it behind more components.

Lesson 4 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/04_managed_vs_build_scorecard.py
Why this matters
Every custom component creates ownership: upgrades, security patches, scaling, backups, observability and
specialist knowledge. Managed services trade some flexibility/control for reduced undifferentiated operations. The
architecture question is where custom control creates enough business value to justify that ownership.
Picture it in your head
Owning a power generator gives control but also fuel, maintenance and failure responsibility. Buying electricity from
the grid gives less control over internals but removes most generator operations. Neither is always right.
New words before we use them

rows: Platform where a provider operates significant infrastructure lifecycle responsibilities.
Management layer that configures/coordinates system behavior.
Ongoing human/system effort to keep a component secure, available and updated.
Cost or difficulty of moving due to APIs, data formats, skills or operational dependencies.
Work required to operate technology but not unique to the business product.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Score choices on required control, compliance, portability, team expertise, uptime responsibility, upgrade burden,
integration, cost and exit plan. 'Managed is expensive' ignores the labor and risk of self-operation. 'Managed is easy'
ignores quotas, platform constraints and provider-specific semantics. The best choice often manages commodity
layers and keeps business-differentiating logic portable.
A second architecture-review lens
A useful total-ownership review includes at least five hidden jobs: upgrades, security response, backups/recovery,
observability/on-call, and capacity planning. Put a named team beside each job. If no team owns it, self-hosting has
an unpriced risk. Managed services also need an exit strategy: identify portable data formats, export/replay
boundaries and provider-specific features you would have to replace. This turns vague lock-in fear into a concrete
migration-cost discussion.

Lesson 5 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/05_bottleneck_capacity_reasoning.py
Why this matters
Scaling is not adding machines everywhere. Throughput is constrained by the narrowest effective boundary: source
API quotas, network, partitions, shuffle, storage write rate, database concurrency, downstream service or even one
serialized key. Scaling the wrong layer increases cost without increasing useful throughput.
Picture it in your head
A highway with eight lanes that narrows to one toll booth still processes cars at roughly the toll-booth rate. Widening
the road before the booth does not solve the bottleneck.
New words before we use them

rows: Useful work completed per unit time.
Elapsed time for one unit/request/event to complete.
Upstream slowing because downstream cannot keep up.
Resource operating near its practical capacity.
Unused capacity reserved for bursts, failures or growth.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Measure stages rather than guessing. Draw source -> ingest -> transform -> storage -> serving. For each, record
capacity, observed throughput, latency, queue depth and limits. Apply simple capacity arithmetic: required throughput
= daily/peak volume divided by useful processing window, adjusted for retries/headroom. Parallelism only helps when
work can be partitioned and downstream accepts it.
A second architecture-review lens
Capacity planning should use percentiles and bursts, not only daily averages. A pipeline averaging 5k events/sec can
still fail when a 10-minute burst hits 40k/sec. Include retry traffic and failure-mode capacity: if losing one partition or
worker makes the remaining system exceed saturation, there is no real headroom. Observe queue depth and lag
because they reveal when arrival rate exceeds service rate even before users see missed deadlines.

Follow with me once
A pipeline must process 36 million events in one hour: 10,000 events/sec average, but design for 2x headroom.
Ingest supports 50k/sec, Spark supports 30k/sec, sink supports 12k/sec. Adding Spark executors cannot meet a

A job runs slowly, so the team doubles compute. The source API is throttled at 500 requests/minute. Cloud cost
doubles while duration barely changes.

validate the original requirement, and finally test a changed case. Architecture recovery should reduce uncertainty,
not hide it behind more components.

Lesson 6 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/06_failure_domain_budget.py
Why this matters
Reliable architecture assumes components fail. The design limits how far a failure spreads, preserves durable
evidence, and defines recovery that can be tested. Availability is an end-to-end property: redundant compute does
not help if every worker depends on one unrecoverable state store or one credential.
Picture it in your head
Ships have watertight compartments so one breach does not sink the whole vessel. Failure domains are architecture
compartments: region, zone, cluster, account, database, partition or deployment boundary.
New words before we use them

rows: Set of components likely to fail together from one cause.
Target time to restore service after disruption.
Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time/state.
Additional components/copies used so one failure need not stop service.
Continuing a reduced but safe service instead of total failure or incorrect output.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Start from business impact, then choose RTO/RPO. Map state: raw source evidence, checkpoints, metadata, serving
tables, secrets and code. Ask what happens if each domain disappears. Multi-zone compute without replicated state
is false comfort. Replication also is not backup: corruption can replicate. Reliable data systems usually combine
durable immutable inputs, idempotent/replayable processing, protected state/checkpoints, tested restore and
controlled publish boundaries.
A second architecture-review lens
Reliability also requires correlated-failure thinking. Two copies in the same account, credential boundary, region, or
deployment can fail together. Ask 'what common thing can kill both?' for every redundancy claim. Recovery plans
should be exercised using known-good evidence: restore a checkpoint copy, replay a bounded raw range, verify key
counts and business totals, then republish. A backup whose restore path is untested is only a hope, not proven
recovery.

Lesson 7 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/07_cost_model.py
Why this matters
Cost is an architecture constraint, not a finance cleanup step. Data systems spend across storage, compute, data
movement, managed-service premiums, observability, redundancy and people. Optimization means paying for
requirements intentionally, not simply choosing the lowest unit price.
Picture it in your head
A cheap printer with expensive ink can cost more over its life than an expensive efficient printer. Architecture cost is
total lifecycle cost and usage shape, not sticker price.
New words before we use them

rows: Total cost of ownership including infrastructure, operations and people.
Cost per useful unit such as TB processed, 1M events or dashboard query.
Data transfer leaving a region/provider/service boundary that may incur cost.
Matching allocated capacity to real workload needs.
Budget/usage rule that triggers review before uncontrolled spend continues.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Create a simple model before optimizing. Separate fixed and variable cost. Measure cost per business-relevant unit
and by environment. Watch data movement: copying the same 20 TB between services can dominate cheap storage.
Reliability has price - replicas and warm standby consume resources - but downtime also has business cost. The
goal is to identify the cheapest architecture that satisfies the requirement set, not to delete reliability controls.
A second architecture-review lens
Cost reviews should protect unit economics from misleading totals. A growing bill can be healthy if business volume
grows faster and cost per million events falls; a flat bill can hide waste if workload shrinks. Attribute spend to
workloads/environments, keep non-production schedules deliberate, and model data movement. Human operating
cost matters too: a technically cheap self-hosted cluster that consumes half an engineer can be more expensive than
a managed service with higher infrastructure charges.

Follow with me once
Option A is serverless query at 5 currency units/TB, scanning 40 TB/day = 200/day. Partitioning/pruning cuts scans to
8 TB/day = 40/day. Option B uses always-on cluster costing 120/day but handles predictable heavy transformations.
Compare workload shape and operations, then model 30-day cost and sensitivity at 2x volume.
What you should see / why it worked
A cost model showing assumptions, unit costs, volume, reliability overhead and a sensitivity case. Cost claims are
traceable rather than 'serverless is cheaper'. The important part is the trace from requirement to decision to evidence;
the same product name can be correct in one requirement set and wrong in another.
Break it: a realistic failure
To save money a team removes duplicate raw retention and keeps only transformed outputs. A later bug cannot be
replayed or audited. The immediate storage saving destroys recoverability and creates much larger incident cost.
Reason through a realistic incident
Preserve the evidence first. State the violated requirement, then identify the smallest failing boundary. Separate
business-data state from compute/configuration/identity state. Bound the blast radius, choose a reversible repair,
validate the original requirement, and finally test a changed case. Architecture recovery should reduce uncertainty,
not hide it behind more components.
Now you do a changed version alone
Build a monthly model for storage, compute, egress and support labor for two architecture options in the supplied
scenario. Identify top two cost drivers and one safe optimization for each.
Fresh changed retry
Double data volume and cut query frequency by half. Recompute rather than assuming your original winner stays
cheapest.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when your decision cites a requirement/constraint and an independent control or measurement.
• If a fact is unknown, label it as an assumption and state what you would measure before committing.
• Reject a design that solves the happy path but has no replay/recovery, ownership, security boundary or cost story.
• After repair/review, change latency, volume, budget or compliance and prove you can adapt instead of reciting the
same diagram.

Lesson 8 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/08_security_governance_matrix.py
Why this matters
Security added at the end becomes a patchwork of broad permissions and manual exceptions. Architecture should
decide identity boundaries, least privilege, encryption, data classification, network paths, auditability, retention and
ownership before data is widely copied.
Picture it in your head
A secure office building is designed with zones, badges, visitor routes, locked rooms and audit cameras. It is harder
to retrofit those boundaries after everyone already has master keys.
New words before we use them

rows: Point where identity, privilege or data exposure changes and requires explicit control.
Multiple independent controls so one failure does not immediately expose the asset.
Collecting/retaining/exposing only data needed for the purpose.
Machine-checkable rules stored and reviewed like code.
Ownership, standards and controls that keep data usable, accountable and compliant.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Draw trust boundaries across source, ingestion identity, raw storage, transform identity, curated serving and
consumers. Prefer workload identity/short-lived credentials over embedded secrets where supported. Separate
admin, producer and consumer privileges. Classify sensitive columns early so masking/tokenization and retention
happen before broad analytics access. Governance also needs ownership, catalog/lineage, quality contracts and
exception processes.
A second architecture-review lens
Security architecture should include the failure path. During incidents, engineers often request broad emergency
access. Define a controlled break-glass mechanism with approval, time limit and audit trail rather than normalizing
permanent admin rights. Governance should also describe change: who can approve a schema change, who owns
quality incidents, how sensitive classification propagates, and how deleted/retained data is proven. Security is an
operating model as well as encryption settings.

Lesson 9 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/09_promotion_foundations_map.py
Why this matters
Job descriptions often mention CDC, data contracts, secrets platforms, data mesh and Kubernetes together. A junior
engineer does not need five specialist certifications before applying, but should understand what problem each
solves, where it fits, and what trade-offs or ownership it introduces. This lesson is a promotion map, not a
replacement for dedicated platform engineering courses.
Picture it in your head
Think of a city map before learning every neighborhood. CDC is a way data changes travel, contracts define
promises at borders, Vault protects secrets/identity material, data mesh changes ownership/product organization,
and Kubernetes is a workload orchestration platform. Knowing the map prevents category mistakes.
New words before we use them

rows: Change Data Capture: publishing/reading inserts, updates and deletes from source change history/logs.
Explicit producer-consumer agreement about schema, semantics, quality and evolution.
System controlling storage/issuance/rotation/access to sensitive credentials and keys.
Sociotechnical approach emphasizing domain ownership, data as product, self-service platform and federated governance.
Platform for orchestrating containerized workloads through declarative desired state and controllers.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
CDC is useful when incremental source changes matter and polling/full reloads are inefficient or too slow; it still
requires ordering, schema evolution, deletes and replay thinking. Data contracts make interface expectations
reviewable before producers silently break consumers. Vault-type systems centralize secret lifecycle and
identity/policy instead of scattering static credentials. Data mesh is mainly an operating/ownership model, not a
database product. Kubernetes can standardize container scheduling, service discovery and desired-state operations
but adds platform complexity; data engineers should not deploy it merely because a pipeline uses containers.
A second architecture-review lens
Use the promotion map to avoid resume-driven architecture. CDC does not remove the need for idempotent
consumers; contracts do not stop every semantic misunderstanding; Vault does not automatically make an
overprivileged application safe; data mesh does not eliminate central platform/governance needs; Kubernetes does
not make a workload scalable by itself. Each concept shifts a specific problem and introduces its own ownership.
Promotion readiness means you can discuss these boundaries clearly and know when deeper specialist study is
required.

Lesson 10 of 10 | Primary practice: 16_M17/practice/architecture_patterns/10_architecture_review_defense.py
Why this matters
Architecture interviews and real design reviews are not drawing competitions. Reviewers want to see whether you
can explain requirements, boundaries, failure behavior, security, cost, alternatives and evidence. A defensible
architecture makes assumptions visible and survives changed conditions without collapsing into 'because this tool is
popular'.
Picture it in your head
A courtroom defense is structured around evidence and reasoning. You must state the claim, support it, acknowledge
weaknesses and explain why alternatives were rejected. Architecture defense is similar, but the goal is collaborative
risk reduction rather than winning an argument.
New words before we use them

rows: Architecture Decision Record: concise record of context, options, decision and consequences.
Belief used by the design that needs validation or a safety margin.
List of important failure/uncertainty items, likelihood/impact and mitigation.
Automated/measurable check that tests an architecture property over time.
Point where evidence must be accepted before promotion/release.

lines.text: Teacher explanation from first principles
Use a repeatable review order: 1 requirements/constraints, 2 data flow and grain, 3 batch/stream/storage choices, 4
failure/replay/state, 5 security/governance, 6 scaling/cost, 7 observability/operations, 8 alternatives/trade-offs, 9
rollout/migration, 10 evidence. Do not hide uncertainty. A strong answer says 'I would measure X before choosing Y'
when the required fact is unknown.
A second architecture-review lens
A mature review explicitly records rejected options. If you choose managed batch, state why streaming or self-hosting
lost under the present requirements. Then define a trigger that would reopen the decision. This protects the team
from cargo-cult architecture and from treating an old ADR as eternal. In interviews, saying 'I would validate peak rate
and consumer latency before finalizing partition count' is stronger than inventing a confident number with no
evidence.
